# Introduction
CDM (Collaborative Decision Making) is a european project who's objective is to fluidify departure flow at compatible airports. This systems enhances a platform's operations in nominal situations and where demand is greater than capacity and, on VATSIM to ease the application on ECFMP (European Collaboration & Flow Management Project) measures.

> There are no illustrating images at this time as the system is still being implemented.
They will be added as soon as revelant images can be captured.
{.is-warning}

# CDM use conditions

The CDM shall be used by default on the following airfields: `LFPG`, `LFPO`, `LFMN`, `LFLL`, `LFBO` et `LFML`.
Any use outside the aerodromes listed above is not permitted. Before opening these aerodromes, <u>it is recommended to have a solid understanding of this document</u>.

Its use is restricted to the lowest open ATC position as follows: `CTR > APP > TWR > GND > DEL`.
As this system integrates regulations for the entire European airspace, it is <u>highly recommended</u> to use it unless you are not confortable with the tool.

> The use of CDM is not assessed as part of a CPT.
{.is-info}

# The core of CDM
PDS (**P**re-**D**eparture **S**equencer) is the main component of CDM.

It is based on information sharing between the various stakeholders and computes a Departure sequence (the order of departures from the parking stand) to streamline outbound traffic while optimizing runway capacity usage.

Its benefits are both economic and environmental, as it helps reduce taxi time by controlling the waiting time at the runway holding point.

PDS is a system that continuously calculates, for each departing aircraft, its engine start-up time, based on all data external to the flight, including:

- Other departing aircraft
- The airport operator: runway capacity
- En-route constraints: regulations / slots
- Traffic flow: controlled runway pressure

## CDM Milestones
### EOBT (Estimated Off Block Time)
To be included in the departure sequence, all IFR traffic must file a flight plan.

This flight plan includes an EOBT (**E**stimated **O**ff-**B**lock **T**ime), i.e., the estimated time of pushback, or, for taxi-out stands, the start of taxi.
This is the simplest (and most readily available) reference time on which PDS can base its calculations.

This timing is found both in your departure list and start-up list under **TOBT**.

> The reason it is found under TOBT is because we use a combination of EOBT and TOBT to apply regulations even on non-CDM airports.
An EOBT becomes a TOBT <u>when it is updated for departure out of a CDM airport</u>.
{.is-info}

All other timings are found in the startup list.This list must be sorted chronologically by TSAT, i.e., from the most imminent to the furthest in time.

### TOBT (Target Off Block Time)
The **T**arget **O**ff-**B**lock **T**ime (TOBT) is the reference time used by PDS and CDM.

It is the target time an aircraft sets as its off-block time (ready for pushback / ready to taxi as soon as clearance is issued). Each aircraft is required to provide a TOBT and keep it updated in order to optimize the departure sequence.

In your EuroScope list, this value may be displayed in different colors depending on its status:

```diagram

```

You can activate a column next to the TOBT named "SET BY", this indicates the origin of the TOBT.
It can have the following two values other than empty (being TOBT from EOBT): `ATC` or `PILOT`.

### TSAT (Target Start-up Approval Time)
The Target Start-Up Approval Time is the sequenced departure (push-back) time, it is calculated by the PDS according to different criteria (runway pressure, CTOT, TOBT...).

The TSAT is the time at which a traffic can expect to be cleared for push (or taxi on nose-out stands) by ATC.
In practice, traffic is sent to the ground frequency once the pilot has reported ready (pilots are asked to be ready 5 minutes prior to their TOBT to ensure a smooth departure flow) and its TSAT is valid.

<p align="center"> The TSAT validity window is <u>+/- 5 minutes</u>.</p>

In case the TSAT is not yet valid when the pilot reports ready, the delivery controller keeps traffic on his frequency until TSAT - 5 minutes.
The pilot may send a new TOBT to depart earlier with no guaranty of an improvement.
If TSAT expires, the pilot **must** send a new one in order to be resequenced.

In Euroscope, TSATs can have different colours each representing a different status as follows :

```diagram

```

In the most optimal conditions, TSAT is the same as TOBT. In case a delay of more than 5 minutes is required, there is startup delay.

The letter just in front of the TSAT indicates the flight plan status and can be three values:
- `P` for **P**lanned when E/TOBT is in more than 35 minutes,
- `C` for **C**orrect when all times are valid,
- `I` for **I**ncorrect when TSAT has expired.

**Optional tool**
There is a toggleable column to the right of the TSAT named TSAC (**T**arget **S**tart-up **A**pproval **C**ommunicated).
This column is used to track TSAT Communicated to the pilot if you would like to provide updates to the pilot yourself in addition to the VDGS website. The column is initially blank and fills with the TSAT currently assigned to the trafic it is communicated to once clicked. It remains green as long as TSAC is within 5 minutes of TSAT.

### TTOT (Target Take-Off Time)
The Target Takeoff Time is the time at which a traffic is expected to reach the runway and depart. It allows the PDS to maintain runway capacity and avoids holding points congestion.
This milestone is only a reference for the PDS and the Tower controller. TTOT is mainly used to determine traffic compliance with downstream calculations and regulations.

For your information : If you notice multiple traffics reaching the holding point after their TTOT, this indicates that the actual departure rate is lower than the optimal one or that the configuration values are not optimised.

### CTOTs (Calculated Take-Off Time)
A slot or CTOT is a time calculated or injected in the CDM that allows compliance with current flow measures and regulations. We then have the following two use cases :

- A major event with slots (eg. Cross The Pond): The CTOTs are calculated in advance and booked a few days/hours prior to the event. In this case we inject the slots in the CDM which will give us the corresponding TSAT.
- An event with flow measures but no bookings : The CDM is restricted by MDIs (Minimum Departure Interval), ADIs (Average Departure Interval) and runway capacity. The CDM calculates a slot (CTOT) compliant with the applicable measure and gives us the appropriate TSAT.

This calculation is transparent to you as ATC but as opposed to a TTOT, a CTOT must be complied with. The concerned traffic must not take-off outside his slot validity window.

<p align="center">The CTOT validity window is<u> -5 to +10 minutes</u>.</p>

In your start-up and departure lists, the CTOT can have different colors indicating the origin of the slot as follows:

```diagram

```

> Only a CTOT due to a flow measure (not orange) can change, the CDM adjusts in real time the slot according to other traffic.
{.is-info}

Next to the CTOT is the "NET" column, it indicates the network status of the flightplan, it can be multiple values as described bellow:

- REA in Yellow to indicate a REA (Ready) Message was sent to find th ebest possible CTOT (only shows if CTOT exists),
- FLS-XXX, this one is a bit trickier as it indicates the **FL**ightplan was **S**uspended (FLS), the second part gives the reason why and can be any of the following:
  - FLS-CDM: Flight Suspension Triggered by CDM (TSAT expired), this will be the most frequent at CDM airports,
  - FLS-MR: Flight Suspended due to Mandatory Route not complied with,
  - FLS-GS: Flight Suspended due to imposed Ground Stop at destination.

# Calculation logic
The PDS is a complex system continuously optimizing the departure sequence. To better understand how it works, let us illustrate different situations.

As soon as traffic connects on ground at an airport where the CDM is in operation, the PDS retrieves the EOBT from the flight plan and displays it as a TOBT. In this case, the TOBT appears in light green (it is further than 5 min from now).

This initial TOBT calculation (estimate) enables PDS to calculate the TTOT as follows:

<p align="center">TOBT + EXOT = TTOT</p>

The EXOT (**E**stimated **T**axi-**O**ut **T**ime) is defined in the airport configuration. The value differs according to the parking area and assigned runway for departure.

The TTOT we just talked about is thus used to check that runway capacity has not been exceeded.

We have 2 different cases: 

- Case 1: runway capacity not exceeded (optimal situation)

- Case 2: runway capacity exceeded

Runway capacity is defined in the airport configuration for normal and low visibility conditions.

---

**Case 1**
If the time difference between two departures is **more** than the hourly capacity reported in minutes, PDS performs the following calculation to determine the TSAT:

<p align="center">TSAT = TTOT - EXOT</p>

---

**Case 2**
If the number of departures is **less** than the hourly capacity reported in minutes, the PDS delays the traffic to the next TTOT complying with the departure rate.

Example for a TTOT at 1157Z. The same TTOT is already "attributed" to another traffic on the same runway thus not complying with the departure rate. The TTOT is shifted by one minute until the departure rate in minutes is complied with.

The PDS then performs the previous calculation with this new TTOT: TSAT = TTOT - EXOT

In this case, the TSAT will differ from the TOBT, and if this difference is greater than 5 minutes, it is referred to as a start-up delay.

---

In addition to this capacity check, the PDS will ensure compliance with ECFMP measures: MDIs (Minimum Departure Interval) and ADIs (Average Departure Interval).

To do so, it first checks that an active measure exists between the departure airport (where the CDM is in operation) and the destination airport. It then checks whether the MDI value is respected between each traffic affected by the measure.

Example: During a Paris By Night event, Frankfurt (EDDF) requires a 6-minute MDI for departures from Charles De Gaulle to Frankfurt. The PDS therefore checks that there are 6 minutes between each departure to Frankfurt.

In this case: The PDS generates a **C**alculated **T**ake **O**ff **T**ime (CTOT), which is used to shift the TTOT of the second departure to the first available slot allowing measure compliance.
The TSAT is then recalculated as follows:

<p align="center">TSAT = CTOT - EXOT</p>

Unlike a CTOT linked to a booking or manually set (orange color), a CTOT imposed to comply with a measure can improve (i.e. reduce the delay out of the block) depending on changes in the TOBTs of the traffic affected by the measure.

# In pratice
To demonstrate the use of CDM from an ATC perspective, we will follow a fictitious departing traffic.

First of all, if you are connected as **the lowest position** at a CDM airport, you must use the command “.cdm master *{ICAO}*”.
This step allows you to interact with the PDS.

To begin, when the traffic connects, the plugin retrieves the flightplan to extract the EOBT. This value will be used by the PDS as explained in the PDS logic section.

> Reminder: Traffic without an EOBT or and IFR flight plan will not be included in the departure sequence.
{.is-info}

Our fictitious traffic will therefore receive a TSAT calculated by the PDS.

## Delivery (DEL)
Your first action will be triggered by the pilot when requesting his departure clearance.
In addition to its clearance, you will need to provide the TSAT as well as its CTOT if applicable.

>TSAT is calculated maximum 35 minutes prior to TOBT, if TOBT is in more than 35 minutes "~" is indicated and no TSAT is to be communicated.
{.is-info}

If the TOBT is expired (RED and NET Sts FLS-CDM), you will then need to ask the traffic to submit a TOBT on the CDM website or provide you with its estimated pushback time and manually add it to the PDS.

> This can be done by clicking on the Red "SEND" field of the last column (MSG) of your start-up list. This sends the pilot a predefined message to update and monitor its CDM/ATFCM status online. If "SEND" is witten in Green, the message was **already sent**.
{.is-info}

If the pilot is unable to enter its own TOBT you can click on the TOBT, a dropdown menu will appear with two options ("Ready TOBT" and "Edit TOBT").
Click on “Edit TOBT” and enter the time provided by the pilot, if the pilot is ready for push you can click "Ready TOBT". This will trigger three actions:

1. Sets TOBT to the actual time
2. Sends a CDM-Network REA Message (for CTOT improvement)
3. Sets the ASRT to the actual time

> When the trafic is ready when requesting clearance, it is best practice to set TOBT **5 minutes in the future** to take into account the time to change frequency and start pushback.
{.is-success}

Later on, when the pilot calls ready for pushback but its TSAT **is not yet valid** (LIGHT GREEN), you will need to note the current time by clicking on its ASRT (**A**ctual **S**tartup **R**equest **T**ime). Once its TSAT becomes valid, you can transfer it to the ground.

As a delivery controller (DEL), at the time of transfer to ground, you must set ASAT (**A**ctual **S**tartup **A**pproval **T**ime) simply by changing the aircraft status to "STUP". The current time will then appear as the ASAT to all other controllers who will be able to see if the traffic has been released by delivery.

## Ground (GND)
As a GND controler, once the traffic sent by DEL is on your frequency, you simply proceed as you normally would; that is, setting "PUSH" status once the traffic is cleared for pushback, this changes the ASAT to GREY as a confirmation.

In the absence of a DEL controller, you must also manage DEL times (TOBT/TSAT/ASAT).

Once the traffic is cleared for pushback and its AOBT (**A**ctual **O**ff-**B**lock **T**ime) is detected by the PDS, no further CDM actions are required. On the ground, you will may need to distribute the traffic to different holding points or sequence them upstream to ensure smooth departures in case of any flow measures or CTOTs.

## Tower (TWR)
Tower must ensure the compliance with CTOTs when they exist.

In coordination with Ground, Tower also monitors the smoothness of departures. Multiple traffics arriving at the holding point after their TTOTs can result from various factors, such as non-optimal taxi times in the configuration, slow taxiing, or excessive waiting at the holding point.

> CDM does not prevent the queue at the holding point. However, proper use of the tool helps to limit it.
The PDS aims to optimize the departure sequence based on the runway capacity that has been defined. It therefore sends the correct number of traffic to the holding point within a defined time window.
{.is-info}
